stream_episodes.pos: Studying the motif of spherical helmet supports encounters similar limitations as the investigation of helmets themselves, albeit to a greater extent. These limitations include the deteriorated state of preservation of the once abundant objects, the imprecise nature of iconography, the scarcity of written sources, and the incomplete nature of existing studies. While conducting a comprehensive analysis of the preservation of modern helmets in European architecture would demand extensive regional research over many years, some insights can be gleaned from a preliminary examination focused on the Silesian area. This examination suggests that approximately 10% of the original number of modern structures have survived. Iconography often lacks the necessary level of detail and accuracy to convey the intricacies of building finials, and written records on the subject are scarce. Nonetheless, research has identified over thirty examples of this type of helmet, both realized and designed, primarily concentrated in the region encompassing the southern Baltic coast, the Danish straits, and the borderlands of Silesia and Lusatia.
stream_episodes.neg: The origins of this motif can be traced back to the forms of obelisks, which were often depicted in iconography as resting on four spheres. Hans Vredeman de Vries, one of the most influential artists of the late 16th century, particularly liked to include them in his compositions. Likely inspired by his work, the architect Hendrik de Keyser replicated the spherical supports at the base of the imperial crown in the design of the Westerkerk tower in Amsterdam. However, the final structure of this building was realized in different forms. Nevertheless, thanks to the publication of the project in the work "Architektura Moderna," the original shape of the tower became possibly more well-known than the final version. This was not the only direction in which the idea of using a sphere as a support could spread throughout Northern Europe. Both Laurens and Hans van Steenwinckel, de Keyser's students, completed crown-like structures for the Danish King Christian IV on the towers of Frederiksborg and Kronborg castles in the early 17th century. From there, they likely spread to the northern regions of Germany, where they were further disseminated directly or through graphics in the direction of Silesia, Lusatia, the Duchy of Prussia, and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

In 1629, a fire at Kronborg Castle in Helsingør on the Sund Strait resulted in the destruction of four out of the five tower helmets. However, the stone finial of Kalkelborg, located on the tower's southeast corner, miraculously survived. This surviving helmet allows us to verify that the rebuilt helmets did not closely resemble their earlier counterparts. During the extensive decade-long reconstruction, Hans van Steenwinckel the younger, the brother of Laurens and also a student of de Keyser, erected a two-tiered, two-story helmet. The first tier of this helmet gives the illusion of being supported by gilded spheres (illustration 3). However, in reality, the spheres were positioned slightly in front of the tambour facets and rested on obelisks. A similar solution was also employed in the helmet of the Barbican in Frederiksborg (illustration 4), which was built by Hans van Steenwinckel the younger between 1621 and 1623. However, in the case of the Barbican, the illusion of the spheres being the support for the upper stories was not utilized. stream_episodes.request: An interesting clue in interpreting the perception of the spherical supports motif is provided by another of the observed objects: Dresden Castle's Hausmannsturm (il. 9). In 1674-8 the existing tower was raised and covered with a new finial designed by Wolf Caspar von Klengel . Both design drawings and variant sketches of the finial have survived . The completed version features a bell-shaped canopy with shell-framed dormers above the cornice, above which rests a low octagonal tambour, a transom and a tier of gilded spheres. The whole is crowned by a concave-profile canopy, a nearly spherical dome with dormers and a slender spire.
